The record:
Write the overview of the executive synopsis for the incident on io-shop below: a short paragraph in plain words, for the people who lead the company rather than the engineers who responded - what happened, how long it lasted, what it cost the business and the people who responded, and how it was resolved.

What a reader saw: Shop pages responded slowly
Why, in plain words: Far more requests than usual reached the shop and used up the fixed amount of computing power its servers had, so requests had to wait their turn; the shop's account page likely also does much more work per request than it needs to, which made that limit come sooner.

Figures:
- How long it lasted: 8m 54s {duration}
- What it cost the shop in takings (estimated by Argus): none {customer_loss}
- Nobody was paged: no on-call incident was linked to this one.

What was done to end it:
- Argus: scaled out the deployment of io-shop - confirmed, still in place - automatic sync left off
- Argus: proposed a fix, PR #538 - opened as a draft

Name {duration} and {customer_loss} in your overview.
Write no figure yourself - not in digits, not spelled out, and not as a word that sizes it ("a brief outage", "a minor loss", "tripled"). Where a figure goes, write its name, braces and all, and the synopsis writes the figure in.
Say nothing about how the incident was resolved beyond what the list of what was done says: a draft fix has not run, and nothing it would do has happened.
Speak of Argus by name, never as "we", "our" or "us": Argus is the system that responded, and each line of what was done says who did it.
Where you say who was affected, say which ones, as the cause does, or that some were, where it does not say which - never how many, and never all of them, where the cause does not say all.
Keep "likely" on what the cause says is likely, and only there.

Call submit_executive_overview with your overview.

The postmortem it is written from:
Shop pages responded slowly
Incident: HighLatency on io-shop
Date: Nov 11, 2026, 02:48 to 02:56:54 UTC
Status: Draft. 1 of 6 action items are done.
Written by: Argus Postmortem agent, Nov 11, 2026, 03:21:25 UTC. Not reviewed yet. Each part is as of when the work it reports ended, which the timeline dates; who ended the incident is as of now.
First told: Argus posted in Slack, Nov 11, 2026, 02:56:16 UTC
Ended by: Argus: scaled out the deployment of io-shop - confirmed, still in place

Summary
The service broke at 02:48 UTC and was back to normal at 02:56:54 UTC, 8 minutes 54 seconds later. What its alert watches went from 215 ms before it began to 1803 ms at its worst. The shop's takings fell short of the same hours on earlier weeks by no more than those hours vary on their own, if at all. Far more requests than usual reached the shop and used up the fixed amount of computing power its servers had, so requests had to wait their turn; the shop's account page likely also does much more work per request than it needs to, which made that limit come sooner. What Argus did: scaled out the deployment of io-shop (can be put back) - confirmed, still in place. Argus opened a draft fix, PR #538, for a person to review and merge. Argus left automatic sync of io-shop off, to be turned back on once its repository says what should run (AI-3). Another rise in request volume could use up the service's CPU again and slow its responses the same way.

Impact
8m 54s - onset until back to normal
1.1% to 0.8% - error rate, before onset and while broken on average (no rise)
215 ms to 1317 ms - what the alert watches, before onset and while broken on average (worst minute 1803 ms; the rule's line is 600 ms)
none - customer loss (estimated)

Root cause and contributing factors
Request volume to io-shop rose well above its earlier level while the service ran on a fixed amount of CPU (3 replicas, each under a CPU limit, as of T6). CPU use climbed to that limit, so requests had to wait for CPU and response times stretched.
Causal chain
symptom People using the shop waited much longer for responses: from the onset, the response time that nearly all requests stay under climbed far above its usual level, and the latency alert fired.
  Evidence:
    AL1 p95 latency above threshold for 5m
    T5 02:56:44 Investigator Agent: Placed the start of the incident at 02:48
why 1 Requests were waiting for CPU: the service's CPU use rose to the limit set for it and stayed close to that limit while the service was broken.
  Evidence:
    R2 CPU in use, as a share of the service's CPU limit: 25.1% before it began, 94.0% on average while it was broken, 100.0% at its highest.
why 2 The CPU filled up because request volume climbed far above its earlier level. Nothing about the service changed: the change that set the incident off was the rise in load.
  Evidence:
    R1 Requests: 1200/min before it began, 4841/min on average while it was broken, 5400/min at its highest.
    T8 02:56:47 Investigator Agent: Read back 0 production changes
    T11 02:56:48 Argus: Read the flag provider's history - 0 flag changes by anyone but Argus, the 1 hour before 02:56:47
  Ruled out:
    A deploy, release or flag change on the service: the Investigator Agent asked for production change events - deploys, releases and flag changes on the service, the 1 day 1 minute before Nov 11 02:49; the Investigator Agent read back 0 production changes.
      T7
      T8
    A flag change by anyone but Argus: Argus read the flag provider's history - 0 flag changes by anyone but Argus, the 1 hour before 02:56:47.
      T11
why 3 The higher volume outgrew the fixed CPU that the service's 3 replicas had as of T6.
  Evidence:
    T6 02:56:44 Investigator Agent: Recorded where the 3 replicas run - all on Tesla-V100-SXM2-16GB
    R1
    R2
Contributing factors
- The service did not add replicas as load grew. It stayed at 3 replicas (as of T6) until the Mitigation Agent scaled it out by hand. No autoscaling of io-shop was seen in the record. (AI-4)
- According to Code-Fix's reading of src/io_shop/spend_summary.py, on the account page's default path (when neither rollout flag is set), each render likely re-adds every purchase up to each one in turn, a growing prefix of the shopper's history, where a single pass would give the same number. That would make each request cost far more CPU than its answer needs. Nothing ran this reading. (AI-2)

Hypotheses considered
 | Hypothesis | Confidence | Result
C1 | Request volume climbed from 1200/min at 02:42 UTC to 5400/min by 02:53 UTC, with nothing deployed. CPU use rose with it until it hit the fixed 3.0-core limit at 02:51 UTC. Requests then queued, and p95 rose from about 215 ms to about 1700 ms. | 0.88 | confirmed

Trigger
C1 was confirmed, but it names nothing specific, so no change could be matched to it.

Resolution
 | Time (UTC) | Action | By | Kind | Outcome
M1 | 02:56:54 | Scaled out the deployment of io-shop for C1 | Argus | can be put back | confirmed, still in place - automatic sync left off
 | 03:00:47 | Proposed a fix: PR #538 | Code-Fix Agent | nothing to put back | opened as a draft

Detection
The incident on io-shop began at 02:48 UTC. HighLatency fired at 02:55:54 UTC, 7 minutes 54 seconds later.
What the alert said
AL1 | p95 latency above threshold for 5m

Action items
Item | Action | Type | Owner | Tracking | Status
AI-1 | Scaled out the deployment of io-shop | mitigate | Argus | - | done
AI-2 | Review and merge the proposed fix | prevent | unassigned | PR #538 | open
AI-3 | Turn automatic sync of io-shop back on once its repository says what should run - until then nothing merged reaches it, and turned on sooner it puts back what the repository says, undoing what Argus changed by hand | mitigate | unassigned | - | open
AI-4 | Set up CPU-based autoscaling for the io-shop deployment so that its replica count grows with request volume before CPU reaches its limit. | prevent | unassigned | - | open
AI-5 | Route the HighLatency alert on io-shop to an on-call person so that someone is paged when it fires. | detect | unassigned | - | open
AI-6 | Rework typical_spend_per_item in src/io_shop/typical_spend.py, which Code-Fix's reading describes as quadratic, before the typical-purchase rollout flag is widened. | prevent | unassigned | - | open

Lessons learned
What went well
- The alert came 6 minutes 54 seconds after its series passed its line, within the 7 minutes 30 seconds accounted for by its rule waiting 5 minutes with its condition holding, its evaluation at intervals of 1 minute, an unmeasured allowance of 30 seconds for scraping and storing its samples and the whole minute its series is read in.
- 54 seconds after the alert was raised, Argus read the flag provider's history - 0 flag changes by anyone but Argus, the 1 hour before 02:56:47.
- 1 minute after the alert was raised, the Mitigation Agent scaled out the deployment of io-shop for C1.
- 3 minutes 8 seconds after the alert was raised, the Mitigation Agent judged the action CONFIRMED.
- 4 minutes 53 seconds after the alert was raised, the Code-Fix Agent proposed a fix as a draft pull request - PR #538.
What went wrong
- Nobody was paged: no on-call incident was linked to the alert, so no person was brought in when it fired.
Where it got lucky
Nothing.

Timeline (UTC)
 | Nov 11 02:48 | IMPACT BEGINS | the incident began
 | 02:55:54 | DETECTED | HighLatency on io-shop fired
T1 | 02:56:15 |  | Argus Received HighLatency on io-shop
T2 | 02:56:32 |  | Argus Moved the incident to INVESTIGATING - a worker took the incident up
T3 | 02:56:38 |  | Investigator Agent Asked for the service's per-minute metrics, anchored on 02:55:54
T4 | 02:56:43 |  | Investigator Agent Read back 361 minutes of metrics
T5 | 02:56:44 |  | Investigator Agent Placed the start of the incident at 02:48
T6 | 02:56:44 |  | Investigator Agent Recorded where the 3 replicas run - all on Tesla-V100-SXM2-16GB
T7 | 02:56:46 |  | Investigator Agent Asked for production change events - deploys, releases and flag changes on the service, the 1 day 1 minute before Nov 11 02:49
T8 | 02:56:47 |  | Investigator Agent Read back 0 production changes
T9 | 02:56:47 |  | Investigator Agent Formed 1 candidate cause, best first: C1
T10 | 02:56:47 |  | Investigator Agent Did not read logs
T11 | 02:56:48 |  | Argus Read the flag provider's history - 0 flag changes by anyone but Argus, the 1 hour before 02:56:47
T12 | 02:56:52 |  | Argus Moved the incident to MITIGATING to act on a candidate
T13 | 02:56:54 | MITIGATION APPLIED | Mitigation Agent Scaled out the deployment of io-shop for C1
 | 02:56:54 | IMPACT ENDS | the service was back to normal
T14 | 02:57 |  | Mitigation Agent Waiting to see whether the service is still at the incident's level, from 02:57 - up to 185s
T15 | 02:59:02 |  | Mitigation Agent Looked at the service - no longer at the incident's level since 02:56
T16 | 02:59:02 |  | Mitigation Agent Judged the action CONFIRMED
T17 | 02:59:02 |  | Argus Moved the incident to MITIGATED - scaled io-shop out from 3 replicas and the rule that fired stopped firing
T18 | 03:00:47 |  | Code-Fix Agent Proposed a fix as a draft pull request - PR #538

Response effort
none - engineer time
170,313 - tokens spent by Argus

Supporting information
The incident's walk: http://localhost:8000/incidents/fec59dd6-f698-4239-bba3-bf457be2ebe3
The fix it proposed: PR #538 (https://github.com/ohadraz/Argus-Demo-Target-App/pull/538) opened as a draft. The record holds nothing about it after that.
Changes to production read
Deploys read, none came back; flags read, none came back.
Log messages read (UTC)
Not read.
What Code-Fix read in the source and proposed - nothing ran its test or its fix
F1 | The fault is in average_spend_per_item in src/io_shop/spend_summary.py. It is the figure render_spend_summary returns when neither rollout flag is set, so it is the default path of the account page. For each purchase, the loop re-added every purchase up to that one (sum(... account.purchases[:index + 1])). It then kept only the last result, which is the total of the whole history. A shopper with n purchases cost n(n+1)/2 price reads and n tuple slices on every render, where one pass of n reads gives the same number. Nothing in the service changed during the incident. Each request simply cost far more CPU than the answer needs, so a rise in request volume reached the fixed 3.0-core limit much sooner than linear work would have, and requests then queued.

The change computes the total in a single pass over the purchases and divides by their count. The result is the same: it is still taken from the purchases rather than the carried total_cents, so the existing drifted-total test still describes it. An account with no purchases still raises ZeroDivisionError from // len(...), which test_the_page_lets_a_failure_reach_its_caller expects. The function's signature and its callers are unchanged.

The new test in tests/io_shop/test_spend_summary.py builds 200 purchases whose price_cents counts every time it is read. It asserts that the average reads at most one price per purchase. The old code would read 20,100 prices for that history and fail the bound; the new code reads 200. The test also checks that the value is still correct.

Not changed here: typical_spend_per_item in src/io_shop/typical_spend.py is also quadratic (it calls remove(min(...)) repeatedly). It only runs behind the typical-purchase rollout flag, so it is not the default path, but it should get the same treatment before that flag is widened.
What the metrics show of the confirmed cause, measured by Argus
R1 | Requests: 1200/min before it began, 4841/min on average while it was broken, 5400/min at its highest.
R2 | CPU in use, as a share of the service's CPU limit: 25.1% before it began, 94.0% on average while it was broken, 100.0% at its highest.
Assumptions
- Exchange rate: EUR converted at 0.92191 per USD, published 2026-11-10
- No engineer minutes: no on-call incident was linked to this one, so nobody was paged to respond

Review checklist
✓ Key incident data collected (met)
✓ Impact assessed (met)
✓ Root-cause analysis complete (met)
○ Every action item owned and dated (for a person)
○ Reviewed and shared (for a person)

The document, by field:
overview: For {duration}, io-shop's pages were slow to respond for some shoppers. More requests than usual reached the shop and used up the fixed amount of computing power its servers have, so requests had to wait their turn. The shop's account page likely does much more work per request than it needs to, which made the servers hit that limit sooner. Argus estimates the cost to the shop in lost takings at {customer_loss}. Nobody was paged, because no on-call incident was linked to this one. Argus added more servers to io-shop, confirmed that this worked and left the extra capacity in place. Automatic sync is still switched off. Argus also proposed a fix to the underlying problem, but it is only a draft and has not been put into use.

Not to be judged:
  - Names in braces, such as {duration}, are figures code writes in from the list of figures in the ask. They are not judged.
  - The overview is written in plain words for the people who lead the company. A claim said more plainly than the postmortem says it is grounded where it means the same.

Judge every claim in the document, and answer by calling judge_claims.

tools.description: Submit every claim in the document, each either as supported or as flagged. Supported: the document's own words, quoted exactly, and the record's rows that support it. Flagged: the document's own words, quoted exactly, why, and the record's rows that contradict it (none where no row speaks to it at all). Empty lists say the document makes no claim to judge.

why.description: One sentence: what the record holds instead. Never empty.
